body_markdown:
Not that long ago, it felt like any and every vintage pickup and 4×4 was bound for greatness, as if the collective enthusiast world had awoken to realize just how charming these machines could be. The good ones hopped on the proverbial grain elevator, and values began to climb seemingly across the board.


But lately, some of the big players in the space have hit a bit of a skid, with values either backsliding or simply running out of that long-held steam. We’re not going to call these “false starts,” per se, but the football analogy works, given the blustery, colder nature of the season and what’s going on with this gathering of classics.


Call it a symptom of a softer, more nuanced collector-car market, or a heat check for a charming but not fully mature segment. Part of what’s intriguing here isn’t just what the values of these familiar classics did in the most recent update, but also how the numbers looked compared to the few years prior.


Here are six familiar SUVs and pickups that stumbled in our most recent update to the Hagerty Price Guide.


## 1988–2000 Chevrolet GMT400


Mecum


**Average decrease: -11%**


One of the most recognizable silhouettes of the late twentieth century, the GMT400 is many people’s choice for “the last great pickup truck.” It has an honesty that newer, more tech-laden trucks often lack. This square, simple design vaulted the GMT400 into collector status quicker than others from the era.


Mecum


Mecum


The rise was quite shocking, really. From 2021–22, the median #2 (Excellent) value of a GMT400 effectively doubled, vaulting from around $15K to roughly $30K. After that one-year launch, values for the GMT400 remained relatively flat. However, the latest update shows a bit of backsliding—now, the median #2 (Excellent) value sits at $25,600.


## 1992–96 Ford Bronco


Mecum


**Average decrease: -5%**


Ford’s big, boxy Bronco is instantly recognizable on the road—for more than just that famous highway chase in California, too. This spacious off-roader was the final iteration of a 30-year run for the nameplate, as Ford mothballed the Bronco badge in 1997, not trotting it out again until 2021.


Mecum


Mecum


That “last of an era” appeal made it a hot item for collectors during the vintage truck and SUV boom of the early 2020s. The median price for a #2 (Excellent) example went from $21,200 in 2019 all the way to $61,000 this spring. But in the most recent update, the median value for that vehicle regressed to $58,000. Whether this is a minor correction or a long-term cooling remains to be seen. That said, that spike and slide is most notable among pristine examples; respectable fifth-gen Broncos are still relatively affordable. Values for condition #3 (Good) have remained a bit steadier, coming in at $15,700 in 2019 and $24,000 today.


## 1973–91 Chevrolet C/K


Mecum


**Average decrease: -4%**


If the GMT400 trucks were the “last great trucks,” then we’d humbly opine that the[Chevrolet C/K](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/square-deal-the-vintage-chevrolet-c-k-pickups-are-classics-you-can-use/) series pickups are the zenith of the form factor. The simple design offered a blank canvas for those who wanted it and a steadfast work companion for those who needed it, while the styling held its own across three different decades. (Heck, we’d submit that the styling still trumps anything you can find on a dealer lot today.)


Mecum


Mecum


Values for these beauties have been on a gradual upward climb since the early 2010s, placing them among the earlier trucks to go from tool to collectible. The biggest runup in median #2 (Excellent) value was a spike from $12,100 at the beginning of 2017 to $20K at the beginning of 2019. But they’ve had two straight quarters of drops, with most versions down 4% this book and most versions down 3% last book.


## 1975–79 Ford F-150


Mecum


**Average decrease: -4%**


The sixth-generation “dentside” Ford F-150 is as good-looking as it is functional. Built atop a chassis that originated in 1965, the dentside was a significant step forward from the previous generation when it came to modern styling. It also gained noteworthy engineering tweaks such as front disc brakes, full double-wall bed construction, and increased use of galvanized steel to better protect it against the dreaded tin worm.


Mecum


Like the Chevy C/K above it, values of these sixth-gen F-150s were already climbing well ahead of the 2020-ish spike in values for a lot of other trucks and SUVs. The biggest jumps came in 2019 and 2021, however. But after peaking last year, this lovable Blue Oval workhorse has tipped downward. Curiously, this backslide focuses primarily on the F-150—other variants of this generation of[F-Series](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/73-79-f-series-values-are-built-ford-tough/) (the F-100, F-250, and F-350) have been faring better than the spec now most common on American roads.


To wit: The median #2 (Excellent) value for the 75–79 F-150 peaked at $47,100 last year, but has since dipped to $41,200 as of the latest update. Drop down a condition rung to the #3 (Good) tier, and you were once looking at $22,500; now, that figure sits at $18,500.


## 1958–83 Jeep CJ-5


Mecum


**Average decrease: -3%**


Transitioning from a military vehicle to a civilian-use machine is not easy—in the former role, functionality won the day, and anything that interfered with that mandate or added cost was shown the door. In the latter, you have to consider whether or not John Q Public actually *enjoyed* their time behind the wheel. But the[Jeep CJ-5](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/your-handy-1955-83-jeep-cj-5-buyers-guide/) marked the company’s launchpad into a machine for the masses, and it’s been widely revered for its success in doing so. For nearly 30 years following its 1955 debut, the CJ-5 marked its territory as the quintessential Jeep.


Mecum


Mecum


That claim to history has made it somewhat of a darling for collectors, as have its simplistic engineering and its relatively reasonable cost of ownership. But—of course you know what’s coming—values for CJ-5s across the board aren’t quite what they once were. In 2023, the median value for a #2 (Excellent) CJ-5 peaked at $26,700; today, that median value rings in at just $16,700. Ouch. A step down the rung, median values for a #3 (Good) example reached as high as $19,400, but now sit at $12,400.


## 1968–83 Toyota FJ40


Mecum


**Average decrease: -3%**


Toyota’s FJ40 Land Cruiser is one of the most recognizable silhouettes in the vintage truck and SUV landscape, and for good reason. It took just two years for the FJ40 to claim the title of best-selling Toyota in America, and the form factor remained largely the same until the model’s departure in 1983.


Mecum


Mecum


Enthusiasts have regarded the[FJ40](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/toyota/land%20cruiser/1974/1974-toyota-land%20cruiser-FJ40) as a darling for quite some time, and our valuation data indicates that it’s one of the earliest SUV/trucks to make the leap to the collectible tier. Case in point: Values for #2 (Excellent) examples were on the rise as early as 2009, and by 2015, that figure had more than tripled. Median condition #1 (Concours) examples peaked in 2015 at a staggering $107,000. But since that peak, values for the FJ40 have been up and down. Per the latest update, the median #2 value now sits at $51,600, which is almost exactly what it was at the start of 2026. Not quite a stumble—more of a stagnation.


Are these value shifts a sign of an overall regression in the vintage truck and SUV market, or is this merely a blip on the longer-term radar for this segment? Only time will tell. Let us know what you think in the comments.
